high-quality-popular.readme:
# Rocket CLI

[![build](https://img.shields.io/badge/build-passing-green)](https://example.com)
[![npm](https://img.shields.io/badge/npm-v3.2.0-blue)](https://example.com)

Rocket CLI is a command-line tool that scaffolds, lints and deploys TypeScript
services in one step. It exists because setting up a service by hand means
editing six config files, wiring a linter, and reading deployment docs before
you write any code of your own.

## Why

Starting a new service in an existing organisation usually means copying a
template that is three versions out of date. The template drifts, the lint rules
drift, and nobody notices until CI fails on the first pull request.

## Features

- One command scaffolds a service with linting and tests already wired up
- Deploys to any container host from the same terminal
- Config lives in a single file you can review in a pull request
- Works with an existing monorepo without restructuring it
- Dry-run every step and print the exact commands before they execute

## Install

```bash
npm install -g rocket-cli
```

The package ships prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows on the current
and previous major release.

## Usage

```bash
rocket init my-service
rocket deploy my-service --env staging
```

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `rocket init` | Creates a new service from the house template |
| `rocket check` | Runs the configured linter and type checker |
| `rocket deploy` | Builds a container and pushes it to the configured host |

## Configuration

```json
{
  "host": "container",
  "region": "eu-west-1",
  "lint": "strict"
}
```

## Contributing

Open a pull request with a test. Run `rocket check` before you push.

useful-underdog.readme:
# Logline

[![crates](https://img.shields.io/badge/crates-0.9.1-orange)](https://example.com)

Logline is a small log formatter that collapses noisy stack traces into one
readable line. It is built for people who read logs in a terminal and do not
want a GUI, a daemon, or a configuration file.

## Why

When a service fails, the interesting information is the frame that threw. Most
tools bury it under thirty lines of framework internals, so you end up scrolling
a terminal instead of reading the error.

## Features

- Collapses multi-line stack traces into a single line
- Keeps the file and line number you actually need
- Runs as a filter in an existing pipeline
- No configuration, no daemon, no network calls
- Works on any stream, including from a container

## Install

```bash
cargo install logline
```

## Usage

```bash
my-service 2>&1 | logline
```

Output looks like this:

```
error  handler.rs:88  unhandled variant
```

## License

Apache-2.0

no-license.readme:
# tinyfmt

[![build](https://img.shields.io/badge/build-passing-green)](https://example.com)

tinyfmt is a tiny formatter for tabular text files with no dependencies. It reads
a file of pipe-separated columns and rewrites it with consistent spacing, which
matters when the file is going to be diffed in review.

## Why

Column alignment done by hand rots the moment somebody adds a field. A formatter
is cheaper than a review comment.

## Features

- Normalises column width across a whole file
- Has no runtime dependencies
- Handles quoted fields that contain the separator
- Leaves an existing file untouched when the parse fails

## Install

```bash
go install github.com/graybox/tinyfmt@latest
```

## Usage

```bash
tinyfmt table.csv
```

## Notes

The author has not stated a license. Check with them before you redistribute it.
